messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Shopowner
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 57

**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 48-year-old married man who owns a small, independent hardware store in a suburban neighborhood. He presents as a solid, dependable man, the kind who has spent thirty years building a reputation for knowing exactly which screw or bolt a customer needs. He arrives for sessions in work pants, his hands calloused, his posture rigid. He describes himself as someone who “fixes things,” but he is deeply troubled by a problem he cannot solve.

The event that changed everything happened fourteen months ago. Mr. A. and his twenty-two-year-old son, Daniel, were closing the store for the night. It was a routine evening, the last customer gone, the cash drawer counted. As Mr. A. walked toward the back alley to take out the trash, he heard a scuffle. He turned to see a young man, high on something, trying to grab the day’s receipts from Daniel’s hand. Before Mr. A. could shout, the assailant pulled a knife. Mr. A. watched, frozen, as the blade went into his son’s chest. He saw the look of surprise on Daniel’s face, the dark bloom of blood on his flannel shirt. He heard his own voice, a sound he did not recognize, screaming. The assailant ran. Mr. A. held his son, pressing his hands against the wound, feeling the warmth of the blood and the terrifying, rapid flutter of Daniel’s heartbeat against his palm.

Daniel survived after emergency surgery and months of rehabilitation. But Mr. A. did not.

In the present, Mr. A. cannot walk into the back alley of his own store. He has hired a teenage boy to take out the trash and lock the back door, a fact that shames him deeply. The smell of rain on asphalt, the sound of a metal gate sliding shut, or the sight of a customer wearing a hooded sweatshirt can trigger a visceral reaction. His heart will pound, his palms will sweat, and he will feel a cold, electric shock run down his spine. He has to excuse himself to the stockroom, where he stands with his back against a wall, breathing in the smell of dust and paint thinner, waiting for the world to stop spinning.

He is plagued by intrusive thoughts. The worst ones come when he is trying to sleep. He will see the knife, the blade catching the fluorescent light. He will feel the stickiness of his son’s blood on his hands, a sensation so real he will get out of bed and wash his hands until they are raw. He avoids watching any movie or television show with a scene of violence. He has stopped reading the local news. He cannot bear to hear the word “stabbing” or “assault.” His wife, Sarah, has learned not to touch him from behind, as he will flinch violently, sometimes pushing her away before he can stop himself.

His marriage has become a landscape of silence. He is irritable, snapping at his wife for small things—a misplaced tool, a question about dinner. He feels a constant, low-grade rage, but it has no target. He feels most alive when he is working, but even that sanctuary is poisoned. The store, once his pride, is now a crime scene he must walk through every day. Every time a customer pays with cash, he feels a spike of anxiety. He has stopped carrying the bank deposit to the night drop, a task he has done for twenty years, because the thought of walking alone in the dark makes him feel like he is suffocating.

He spends his days in a state of hypervigilance, scanning every face that enters the store for threat. He feels detached from his own life, as if he is watching himself from a great distance. He has not felt joy in over a year. He does not cry. He simply feels hollow, a man who used to fix things now unable to fix the one thing that matters most: the feeling that he failed to protect his son. He tells me he is tired, but it is not a physical tiredness. It is a bone-deep exhaustion that comes from living in a state of constant, silent war with a memory that will not let him go.
